metadata.hierarchy_note: hierarchy reflects data/ck3_title_tree.json (save-derived de jure tree including x_script_* dynamic titles); downstream localisation/historicity mods should key on barony_key and join against their target landed_titles tree.

schema_notes.vanilla_ck3_name: Exact English localisation string from CK3 titles_l_english.yml.
schema_notes.modern_name: Clean modern/standard English display name of the audited settlement or holding (stripped of key prefixes and parenthetical notes).
schema_notes.modern_name_note: Optional administrative parent, alternate designation, or native-script qualifier extracted from modern_name; null if none.
schema_notes.hierarchy: De jure title hierarchy from data/ck3_title_tree.json (empire, kingdom, duchy, county, holding_type).
schema_notes.anachronism_type: Mutually exclusive historicity category: attested_pre_867 | fictional_placeholder | post_867_eponym | renamed_post_867 | modern_anachronism | early_modern_foundation | high_late_medieval_attestation | unattested_indigenous_or_minor.
schema_notes.is_historical_at: Bookmark-keyed booleans {'867', '1066', '1178'}: true iff first_mention_year is known and <= that bookmark year.
schema_notes.first_mention_year: Integer year of earliest documented attestation for the audited name (negative values = BCE; null if unattested).
schema_notes.first_mention_attestation: Summary of earliest documented textual or epigraphic attestation (or unattested status).
schema_notes.eponym: Structured eponym object {year, post_867, type, details} when named after a person, saint, ruler, deity, or dynasty/tribe; null otherwise.
schema_notes.natural_proper_name: Object indicating whether the title derives from a hydronym, oronym, choronym, or topographic_feature.
schema_notes.morphemes: List of constituent roots/morphemes with form, language, language_code (ISO 639-3 / ISO 639-5), and translation.
schema_notes.etymology_analysis: Linguistic and historical etymology of the audited barony name.
schema_notes.historical_names: List of distinct pre-867 attested names for the same site or immediate predecessor: [{name, native_script, language, attested_from, attested_to, source, relationship, notes}].
schema_notes.source_url: Primary reference URL (Wikipedia or regional historical encyclopedia), or null if unavailable.

b_calafat.first_mention_attestation: First documented in a 1424 charter issued by Wallachian Prince Dan II; settled earlier in the 14th century by Genoese colonists as a Danube ship-repair station.

morphemes.translation: caulking / place where ships are tarred

b_calafat.etymology_analysis: According to historian Nicolae Iorga, the toponym derives from Byzantine Greek Kalafatis (referring to caulkers or a personal name), meaning 'place where ships are tarred', reflecting its medieval role as a Danube ship-repair and customs port.

b_cujmir.first_mention_attestation: No documented medieval attestation prior to the early modern period; the historic village church in Cujmir dates to 1715.
b_cujmir.etymology_analysis: Romanian rural toponym of Oltenia (Mehedinți County), likely of South Slavic or regional anthroponymic origin, unattested in written records before the modern/early modern era.

b_strehaia.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 1471 as an estate of the Craiovești boyars, later serving as a residence of the Bans of Oltenia.
b_strehaia.etymology_analysis: Toponym from South Slavic / Romanian streha ('eaves, shelter'), reflecting its medieval role as a fortified boyar court and refuge in the Motru River valley.

b_segarcea.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in writing in 1557 in a charter issued by Wallachian Prince Pătrașcu cel Bun.
b_segarcea.etymology_analysis: Wallachian settlement name in Dolj County attested from the 16th century; local tradition links it to fertile agricultural land, though its exact linguistic origin is uncertain.

b_craiova.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 1475 in Wallachian charters as the seat of the Great Ban of Craiova.
b_craiova.etymology_analysis: Derived either from Old Slavonic kral ('king', borrowed into Romanian as crai) or krajina ('border, edge') with the Slavic toponymic suffix -ova.

historical_names.name: Pelendava
historical_names.source: Tabula Peutingeriana (c. 225 CE)
historical_names.notes: Ancient Dacian and Roman settlement of Pelendava located at modern Craiova (Cârligei-Bucovăț).

b_corabia.first_mention_attestation: Founded as a modern Danube port town by royal decree in 1871.
b_corabia.etymology_analysis: Named after Romanian corabie ('ship, vessel'), reflecting its establishment as a Danube grain-export port.

historical_names.name: Sucidava
historical_names.source: Constantine's Bridge inauguration (328 CE) and Tabula Peutingeriana
historical_names.notes: Ancient Dacian and Roman fortress-town of Sucidava (in modern Celei, Corabia), linked across the Danube to Oescus by Constantine's Bridge in 328 CE.

b_dragasani.first_mention_attestation: First documented on June 7, 1535 in a chrysobull issued by Wallachian Prince Vlad Vintilă.
b_dragasani.etymology_analysis: Formed from the personal name Drăgaș (ultimately Slavic drag, 'dear') plus the Romanian collective/toponymic suffix -ani ('people/descendants of Drăgaș').

historical_names.name: Rusidava
historical_names.source: Tabula Peutingeriana (c. 225 CE)
historical_names.notes: Dacian settlement and Roman fort of Rusidava on the Olt road between Sucidava and Arutela, within modern Drăgășani.

b_severin.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 1233 with the appointment of Luca, the first Ban of Severin, under the Kingdom of Hungary.
b_severin.etymology_analysis: Medieval Severin derives either from Old Church Slavonic severno ('northern', i.e. north of the Danube) or from Saint Severinus of Noricum (d. 482 CE), patron saint of the medieval colony; 'Drobeta' was prefixed in 1972 from the ancient Roman city.

historical_names.name: Drobeta
historical_names.source: Trajan's Bridge construction (103–105 CE) and Ptolemy's Geographia (c. 150 CE)
historical_names.notes: Ancient Dacian town and Roman castrum/municipium of Drobeta at the northern end of Trajan's Bridge.

b_orsova.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in medieval written records in 1150 under the name Ursoua.
b_orsova.etymology_analysis: Medieval toponym attested from 1150 as Ursoua (later Hungarian Orsova, Romanian Orșova), possibly via Slavic adaptation near the Cerna-Danube confluence.

historical_names.name: Dierna
historical_names.source: Trajanic Roman fort (c. 106 CE), Ptolemy's Geographia, and Tabula Peutingeriana
historical_names.notes: Roman fort and municipium of Dierna/Tierna beneath historic Orșova at the mouth of the Cerna River.

historical_names.name: Tierna
historical_names.source: Trajanic Roman fort (c. 106 CE), Ptolemy's Geographia, and Tabula Peutingeriana
historical_names.notes: Roman fort and municipium of Dierna/Tierna beneath historic Orșova at the mouth of the Cerna River.

b_mehadia.first_mention_attestation: First recorded in 1323 as Michald in Hungarian royal documents, and in 1376 as the seat of a Romanian district.
b_mehadia.etymology_analysis: Most linguists derive Mehadia from medieval Hungarian Miháld (personal name Mihály + -d suffix, attested 1323), while an alternative hypothesis links it to Roman Ad Mediam.

historical_names.name: Ad Mediam
historical_names.source: Trajanic fort (101 CE) and Tabula Peutingeriana
historical_names.notes: Roman military camp and civilian settlement (Ad Mediam / Praetorium) in the Cerna valley.

historical_names.name: Praetorium
historical_names.source: Trajanic fort (101 CE) and Tabula Peutingeriana
historical_names.notes: Roman military camp and civilian settlement (Ad Mediam / Praetorium) in the Cerna valley.

b_karansebes.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 1289 in a charter of King Ladislaus IV of Hungary.
b_karansebes.etymology_analysis: Compound of Karán (derived by Frigyes Pesty from Old Hungarian Kavarán, or from a pre-Hungarian root) and Sebes ('swift', from the Sebeș River at its confluence with the Timiș).

historical_names.name: Tibiscum
historical_names.source: Ptolemy's Geographia (c. 140–150 CE) and Tabula Peutingeriana
historical_names.notes: Major Roman fort and municipium of Tibiscum located at Jupa, 5 km north of Caransebeș (administered by the modern city).

b_targu_jiu.first_mention_attestation: First officially recorded in 1406 under the name Jiul in a charter of Wallachian Prince Mircea the Elder.
b_targu_jiu.etymology_analysis: Romanian compound meaning 'Market on the Jiu', combining târg ('market', from Slavic trŭgŭ) with the Jiu River.

b_baia_de_arama.first_mention_attestation: First documented as a village in 1581, later developing as a copper-mining market town.
b_baia_de_arama.etymology_analysis: Romanian descriptive toponym meaning 'Copper Mine', from baie ('mine') and aramă ('copper').

b_brasso.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned as Corona in the 1235 Catalogus Ninivensis; the name Barasu (Brassó/Brașov) is attested in 1252 in Terra Saxonum de Barasu.
b_brasso.etymology_analysis: Derived either from Turkic barasu ('white water') with Slavic suffix -ov, or from the local Bârsa River adapted into Slavic as Barsov/Brașov; Latin Corona and German Kronstadt mean 'Crown City'.

historical_names.name: Cumidava
historical_names.source: Roman epigraphic attestation (2nd century CE)
historical_names.notes: Ancient Dacian-Roman fort Cumidava at nearby Râșnov in the Brașov Depression.

b_balvanyos.first_mention_attestation: Mentioned in written sources from the 12th century onward as Baluanus, and later in 1360 as Castrum Balwanus.
b_balvanyos.etymology_analysis: Hungarian bálványos ('idolatrous, having idols'), referring in local tradition to the Apor lords holding out there as pagans after Hungary's Christianization.

b_sepsiszentgyorgy.first_mention_attestation: First documented in the 1332 papal tithe register as Sacerdos de Sancto Georgio.
b_sepsiszentgyorgy.etymology_analysis: Hungarian Sepsiszentgyörgy combines the Székely seat name Sepsi with Szentgyörgy ('Saint George'), translated into Romanian as Sfântu Gheorghe.

b_kovaszna.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1548 under the form Kowazna.
b_kovaszna.etymology_analysis: Widely derived from Slavic kvas ('sour, bitter'), referring to the town's effervescent mineral water springs.

b_beszterce.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1241 as oppidum Nosna / Markt Nosa in accounts of the Mongol invasion, and in 1264 as Villa Bistiche.
b_beszterce.etymology_analysis: Named after the Bistrița River, from Slavic bystrica ('fast-moving water'); Hungarian Beszterce and German Bistritz are adaptations of the same hydronym.

b_radna.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 1235 as a major Transylvanian silver-mining center prior to its destruction by the Mongols in 1241.
b_radna.etymology_analysis: From Slavic ruda ('ore, metal') / rudna ('ore-bearing'), reflecting its medieval silver and lead mines.

b_des.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 1061 and 1214 under the name Dees.
b_des.etymology_analysis: Romanian Dej is borrowed from Hungarian Dés, itself derived from the personal name Desiderius.

b_szek.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 1291 in a charter referring to 'hospites nostri de Zek'.
b_szek.etymology_analysis: Romanian Sic derives from Hungarian Szék ('seat, chair/administrative seat'), an important medieval salt-mining town.

b_laposbanya.first_mention_attestation: First documented as Lápos-Bánya in 1630, though mining activity in the area is recorded from 1315.
b_laposbanya.etymology_analysis: Hungarian Láposbánya means 'Lăpuș Mine' (after the Lăpuș River and local gold/iron mines); modern Romanian Băiuț is a diminutive of baie ('mine').

b_feher.first_mention_attestation: Often dated to c. 950 CE as Civitas Alba via retrospective 13th-century chronicle tradition (Gesta Hungarorum) rather than a contemporary 950 CE document; firmer contemporary 11th-century charters attest Fehérvár / Alba (e.g., 1097 CE; built on Roman Apulum).
b_feher.etymology_analysis: Hungarian Fehérvár (later Gyulafehérvár), Slavic Bălgrad, German Weißenburg, and Latin Alba all mean 'White Citadel', referring to the white stone ruins of Roman Apulum.

historical_names.name: Apulum
historical_names.source: Ptolemy's Geographia (c. 150 CE) and Roman Trajanic legionary inscriptions
historical_names.notes: Dacian fortress Apoulon and major Roman legionary base and municipium/colonia Apulum at modern Alba Iulia.

historical_names.name: Apoulon
historical_names.source: Ptolemy's Geographia (c. 150 CE) and Roman Trajanic legionary inscriptions
historical_names.notes: Dacian fortress Apoulon and major Roman legionary base and municipium/colonia Apulum at modern Alba Iulia.

b_kukullovar.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in a 1177 charter as villa Cuculiensis castri, referring to the early Árpád-era earth fort.
b_kukullovar.etymology_analysis: Hungarian Küküllővár means 'Castle on the Küküllő (Târnava) River'; Romanian Cetatea de Baltă ('Marsh Fortress') refers to its marshy valley setting.

b_abrudbanya.first_mention_attestation: First recorded in 1271 under the form terra Obruth.
b_abrudbanya.etymology_analysis: Named after the Abrud River (attested 1271 as Obruth, possibly from a Dacian root for gold); Hungarian Abrudbánya adds bánya ('mine').

historical_names.name: Alburnus Maior
historical_names.source: Roman wax tablets of Alburnus Maior (131–167 CE)
historical_names.notes: Roman castellum at Abrud defended the nearby 2nd–3rd century CE gold-mining settlement of Alburnus Maior (Roșia Montană).

b_nagyszeben.first_mention_attestation: First recorded in a December 20, 1191 papal document of Celestine III as Cibinium.
b_nagyszeben.etymology_analysis: Sibiu / Hungarian Nagyszeben ('Great Sibiu') derives from Bulgar-Turkic Sibin (< Sebin); the German name Hermannstadt means 'Hermann's town', after the 12th-century Saxon colonist leader Hermann of Nuremberg.

historical_names.name: Cedonia
historical_names.source: Tabula Peutingeriana (c. 225 CE)
historical_names.notes: Roman settlement of Cedonia located in the Sibiu / Gușterița area prior to the 12th-century Saxon foundation.

b_alvinc.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 1206 in royal privilege records of Transylvanian guest settlers, and granted to the Chapter of Esztergom in 1219 as Alvinc.
b_alvinc.etymology_analysis: Hungarian Alvinc ('Lower Vinc') and Romanian Vințu de Jos ('Lower Vinț') distinguish it from Felvinc (Unirea), derived from the personal name Vincentius.

b_szaszkezd.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 1309 under the form Kyzd.
b_szaszkezd.etymology_analysis: Hungarian Szászkézd ('Saxon Kézd') reflects the replacement of earlier Székely settlers (Kézd) by Transylvanian Saxons (Keisd), adapted into Romanian as Saschiz.

b_fogaras.first_mention_attestation: First attested as Terra Blacorum in 1222; the Făgăraș Citadel was built around 1310.
b_fogaras.etymology_analysis: Proposed etymologies include Pecheneg fagar šu ('ash-tree water'), Romanian *făgar ('beech forest', from fag), or Hungarian fogoly ('partridge').

b_torcsvar.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 1212 as the Teutonic wooden castle Dietrichstein (lapis Theoderici); the stone castle (Törzburg / Törcsvár) was chartered in 1377.
b_torcsvar.etymology_analysis: Hungarian Törcsvár and German Törzburg refer to the fortified mountain-pass castle (built by Saxons in 1377 on the site of the 1212 Teutonic Dietrichstein); Romanian Bran means 'gate/border'.

b_vajdahunyad.first_mention_attestation: First recorded in 1265 as Hungnod (and 1278 as Huniad; 1409 Hwnyadwar; 1575 Vayda Hunyadi).

eponym.details: Hungarian 'Vajdahunyad' ('Voivode Hunyad', attested 1575) refers directly to John Hunyadi (c. 1406–1456), Voivode of Transylvania and Regent of Hungary, whose family was granted Hunyad Castle in 1409.

b_vajdahunyad.etymology_analysis: Romanian Hunedoara is an adaptation of Hungarian Hunyadvár ('Hunyad Castle'), while Hungarian Vajdahunyad ('Voivode Hunyad') directly honors John Hunyadi, Voivode of Transylvania.

b_harszoc.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the 1247 Diploma of the Joannites as terra Harszoc.
b_harszoc.etymology_analysis: Attested in 1247 as Latinized terra Harszoc (later Hatzak 1276, Hungarian Hátszeg, Romanian Hațeg), traditionally interpreted in Hungarian as hát ('back') + szeg ('corner').

historical_names.name: Ulpia Traiana Sarmizegetusa
historical_names.source: Roman foundation charter under Emperor Trajan (106–110 CE)
historical_names.notes: Capital of Roman Dacia located in the Hațeg Depression (Țara Hațegului), ~15 km west of modern Hațeg.

b_deva.first_mention_attestation: First recorded in 1269 as castrum Dewa in a privilege grant of King Stephen V of Hungary.
b_deva.etymology_analysis: First attested in 1269 as castrum Dewa; proposed etymologies include Dacian dava ('fortress'), PIE *dhewa ('settlement'), or Slavic/Hungarian roots.

b_szekelyudvarhely.first_mention_attestation: First documented in a 1334 papal register of duties as sacerdos de Oduorhel.
b_szekelyudvarhely.etymology_analysis: Hungarian Székelyudvarhely means 'Székely Courtyard Place' (Udvarhely attested 1334; Székely- prefixed by 1615); Romanian Odorheiu Secuiesc adapts the Hungarian name.

b_marosvasarhely.first_mention_attestation: First recorded in the 1332 papal tithe registry under the Latin name Novum Forum Siculorum ('New Szekler Marketplace').
b_marosvasarhely.etymology_analysis: Hungarian Marosvásárhely ('Mureș Marketplace') and Romanian Târgu Mureș ('Mureș Market') both refer to the medieval Székely market town on the Mureș River.

b_csikszereda.first_mention_attestation: First authentically documented as a market town (oppidum) on August 5, 1558 in a privilege charter issued by Queen Isabella.
b_csikszereda.etymology_analysis: Hungarian Csíkszereda and Romanian Miercurea Ciuc both mean 'Wednesday [Market] of Ciuc', referring to the weekly Wednesday market held in the Csík basin.

b_gyergyoszentmiklos.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1332 in the papal tithe register.
b_gyergyoszentmiklos.etymology_analysis: Hungarian Gyergyószentmiklós combines the regional basin name Gyergyó with Szentmiklós ('Saint Nicholas'), the patron saint of its medieval church.

b_torda.first_mention_attestation: First appears in written sources in 1075 under the name castrum Turda.
b_torda.etymology_analysis: Attested in 1075 as castrum Turda (Hungarian Torda, Romanian Turda), derived from an early Hungarian personal or clan name Torda.

historical_names.name: Potaissa
historical_names.source: Milestone of Aiton (108 CE) and Ptolemy's Geographia (c. 150 CE)
historical_names.notes: Dacian settlement and Roman legionary fortress (Legio V Macedonica) and colonia of Potaissa at modern Turda.

historical_names.name: Patavissa
historical_names.source: Milestone of Aiton (108 CE) and Ptolemy's Geographia (c. 150 CE)
historical_names.notes: Dacian settlement and Roman legionary fortress (Legio V Macedonica) and colonia of Potaissa at modern Turda.

b_banffyhunyad.first_mention_attestation: 1332 CE, papal tithe register as Sacerdos de Villa Hunad (Bánffy family became landlords in 1330 CE).

eponym.details: Named after the Hungarian Bánffy noble family, who became landlords of the town in 1330 CE (giving the Hungarian name Bánffyhunyad).

b_banffyhunyad.etymology_analysis: Hungarian compound combining the Bánffy noble family name (landlords from 1330 CE) with the earlier settlement name Hunyad (attested 1332 CE as Villa Hunad; Romanian Huedin).

b_koloszvar.first_mention_attestation: 1213 CE, Medieval Latin royal charter as Castrum Clus (Hungarian Kulusuar first recorded in 1246 CE).

morphemes.translation: enclosed place/valley (from Latin clusa / Slavic ključ) or personal name Miklós

b_koloszvar.etymology_analysis: Hungarian Kolozsvár (first recorded 1246 CE as Kulusuar) combines Kolozs (linked to Latin clusa 'enclosed place' or Slavic ključ, or personal name Miklós) with vár ('castle'). Built on the site of ancient Dacian-Roman Napoca.

historical_names.name: Napoca
historical_names.source: Roman milestone discovered near Cluj (c. 106–108 CE); Ptolemy's Geographia (2nd century CE)
historical_names.notes: Pre-Roman Dacian settlement and Roman provincial capital of Dacia Porolissensis, evacuated in 274 CE.

historical_names.name: Municipium Aelium Hadrianum Napoca
historical_names.source: Roman milestone discovered near Cluj (c. 106–108 CE); Ptolemy's Geographia (2nd century CE)
historical_names.notes: Pre-Roman Dacian settlement and Roman provincial capital of Dacia Porolissensis, evacuated in 274 CE.

historical_names.name: Colonia Aurelia Napoca
historical_names.source: Roman milestone discovered near Cluj (c. 106–108 CE); Ptolemy's Geographia (2nd century CE)
historical_names.notes: Pre-Roman Dacian settlement and Roman provincial capital of Dacia Porolissensis, evacuated in 274 CE.

b_szaszregen.first_mention_attestation: 1228 CE, charter of King Andrew II of Hungary as Regun.
b_szaszregen.etymology_analysis: Hungarian Szászrégen ('Saxon Reghin', German Sächsisch-Regen) prefixes Szász ('Saxon', referring to Transylvanian Saxon settlers) to the medieval settlement name Regun (attested 1228 CE).

b_aranyosbanya.first_mention_attestation: 1325 CE, royal mining privilege charter of King Charles I of Hungary.

morphemes.translation: golden (from arany 'gold', referring to the Arieș River)

b_aranyosbanya.etymology_analysis: Hungarian Aranyosbánya ('Gold-river Mine', Romanian Baia de Arieș) combines Aranyos ('golden', the Hungarian name of the Arieș River, attested 1075 CE) with bánya ('mine'), reflecting its medieval gold mining charter of 1325 CE.

b_targoviste.first_mention_attestation: 1396 CE, travelogue of Bavarian soldier Johann Schiltberger (published 1427 CE), mentioning Târgoviște alongside Argeș as Wallachian capitals.
b_targoviste.etymology_analysis: From South Slavic *tŭrgovište ('marketplace, market town'), combining tŭrgŭ ('market') and the locative suffix -ovište.

b_campulung.first_mention_attestation: 1300 CE, Latin funerary inscription of Comes Laurencius de Longo-Campo in the Bărăția Church, Câmpulung.
b_campulung.etymology_analysis: Romanian Câmpulung ('Long Field', calqued in Medieval Latin as Longus-Campus / Longo-Campo, Old Church Slavonic Dlăgopole, and German Langenau).

b_arges.first_mention_attestation: 1330 CE, Hungarian royal chronicles documenting King Charles I of Hungary's campaign against Basarab I and the Argeș stronghold.
b_arges.etymology_analysis: Named after the Argeș River (related to Thracian/Dacian *Argesos, recorded by Herodotus in the 5th century BCE as Ordesos); the fortified town of Argeș (later Curtea de Argeș) is first attested in 1330 CE.

b_pitesti.first_mention_attestation: 1386 CE (20 May 1386), charter issued by Voivode Mircea the Elder of Wallachia.
b_pitesti.etymology_analysis: Romanian patronymic toponym formed from a personal name (Pitea) and the collective/settlement suffix -ești.

b_polovragi.first_mention_attestation: 1480 CE (18 January 1480), Wallachian chrysobull (hrisov) issued by Voivode Basarab cel Tânăr.
b_polovragi.etymology_analysis: Toponym of uncertain origin, variously linked in scholarship to Slavic or Dacian substrate elements.

b_govora.first_mention_attestation: 1485 CE (27 September 1485), Wallachian chrysobull attesting Govora Monastery (settlement attested 1488 CE).

morphemes.translation: murmuring spring/stream (from Slavic govoriti 'to speak, murmur')

b_govora.etymology_analysis: Derived from South Slavic *govoriti ('to speak, murmur'), referring to the murmuring mineral springs (or Thracian-Dacian 'valley with springs').

morphemes.translation: personal or family name (associated with the Filișanu boyar family)

b_filiasi.etymology_analysis: Romanian plural settlement name derived from the personal/clan name Filiaș (associated with the Filișanu boyars).

b_tabla_butii.first_mention_attestation: 1211–1225 CE, Teutonic Knights' fortification (Cruceburg / Cetatea Buzăului) in the Tabla Buții mountain pass.
b_tabla_butii.etymology_analysis: Romanian compound meaning 'the plaque/board of the barrel', referring to the stamped customs plaques applied to merchant barrels passing through the Wallachia–Transylvania border checkpoint.

b_zoresti.etymology_analysis: Romanian patronymic toponym from the personal name Zor (hypocoristic of Lazor) + settlement suffix -ești.

b_dumbraveni.first_mention_attestation: 1789 CE, Battle of Rymnik (near Plăinești, former name of Dumbrăveni, Vrancea; surrounding commune villages attested from the 16th century).
b_dumbraveni.etymology_analysis: Romanian settlement name from dumbravă ('oak grove', borrowed from Slavic *dǫbrava) + inhabitants suffix -eni.

b_cetatea_alba.first_mention_attestation: c. 1290 CE, Genoese commercial records (as Moncastro / Maurokastron; attested as Romanian Cetatea Albă and Slavic Bilhorod by the 14th century).
b_cetatea_alba.etymology_analysis: Romanian Cetatea Albă ('White Citadel', parallel to Slavic Bilhorod / Belgorod 'White City' and Turkish Akkerman) arose in the High Middle Ages on the ruins of the ancient Greek colony Tyras.

historical_names.name: Tyras
historical_names.source: Classical Greek sources (founded c. 6th century BCE by Milesian colonists)
historical_names.notes: Ancient Greek colony on the Dniester Estuary, later under Roman and Byzantine rule until destroyed in the 4th century CE.

b_tighina.first_mention_attestation: 1408 CE (8 October 1408), Old Church Slavonic commercial grant of Moldavian Voivode Alexander the Good (as Tyagyanyakyacha; Tighina appears in the late 15th century).

morphemes.translation: medieval settlement name (from Cuman Tyagyanyakyacha; later renamed Bender from Persian bandar 'port')

b_tighina.etymology_analysis: First attested in 1408 CE under the Cuman-origin name Tyagyanyakyacha, evolving into Romanian Tighina (Genoese Teghenaccio) before Ottoman conquest in 1538 CE renamed it Bender (Persian bandar 'port').

b_chilia.first_mention_attestation: 1241 CE, Persian chronicle of Rashid-al-Din Hamadani (recording Byzantine Greek Kellia 'granaries' for Chilia Veche; Kiliia / Chilia Nouă developed in the 14th–15th centuries).
b_chilia.etymology_analysis: From Byzantine Greek κελλία (kellia, 'granaries, storehouses'), first recorded in 1241 CE.

b_oblucita.first_mention_attestation: 1574 CE, Moldavian/Ottoman chronicles (as Oblucița / Obluchitsa; Arab geographer Abulfeda recorded Saecdji in the 14th century).
b_oblucita.etymology_analysis: Romanian Oblucița (Bulgarian Obluchitsa) derives from South Slavic *oblutak ('water-rounded stone/pebble') + -ița, arising post-867 on the site of the ancient Celtic-Roman fortress Noviodunum.

historical_names.name: Noviodunum
historical_names.source: Roman military records of Moesia (46 CE); Jordanes' Getica (551 CE)
historical_names.notes: Ancient Celtic-Roman fortress ('New Fort') serving as main base of the Classis Flavia Moesica on the Lower Danube; abandoned after 681 CE.

b_artsyz.first_mention_attestation: 1816 CE, founded as a German colonist settlement ('No. 14', later Alt-Arcis / Artsyz) in Bessarabia.

morphemes.translation: named after the French town of Arcis-sur-Aube (site of an 1814 battle)

b_artsyz.etymology_analysis: Founded in 1816 CE by German colonists in Bessarabia and named in 1819 CE after Arcis-sur-Aube in France, site of an 1814 Napoleonic battle.

b_lapusna.first_mention_attestation: 1454 CE (25 August 1454), Moldavian document attesting vama Lăpușna (the Lăpușna River is attested from 1430 CE).
b_lapusna.etymology_analysis: Named after the Lăpușna River (attested 1430 CE), from South Slavic *lopuš ('burdock, butterbur') + -na.

b_chisinau.first_mention_attestation: 1436 CE (17 July 1436), Moldavian charter issued by Voivodes Iliaș and Ștefan II.

morphemes.translation: spring/watering place (from Old Romanian chișla nouă 'new spring' or Hungarian Kisjenő)

b_chisinau.etymology_analysis: Debated etymology: either from Old Romanian chișla nouă ('new spring', with Turkic/Pecheneg kıșla) or from Hungarian Kisjenő ('Little Jenő').

morphemes.translation: name of the Tigheci forest and river

b_tigheci.etymology_analysis: Named after the Codrii Tigheciului ('Tigheci Forest') and Tigheci River; settlement first attested in 1436 CE as Chigheci.

b_cahul.first_mention_attestation: 1502 CE (2 July 1502), Moldavian chancery document (as Șcheia; later Frumoasa in 1716 CE, renamed Cahul in 1835 CE).

morphemes.translation: named after the 1770 Battle of Kagul (from the Kagul River/Lake)

b_cahul.etymology_analysis: First attested in 1502 CE as Șcheia and in 1716 CE as Frumoasa; renamed Cahul in 1835 CE after the 1770 Battle of Kagul.

b_dorohoi.first_mention_attestation: 1408 CE, treaty between Moldavian Voivode Alexander the Good and King Władysław II Jagiełło of Poland.

morphemes.translation: settlement name (from Slavic dorog 'dear' or doroga 'road')

b_dorohoi.etymology_analysis: East Slavic-origin toponym (linked to *dorog 'dear' or *doroga 'road'), first attested as a Moldavian customs and market town in 1408 CE.

b_harlau.first_mention_attestation: 1384 CE (1 May 1384), Moldavian document attesting the princely court of Lady Margareta (Mușata) at Hârlău.
b_harlau.etymology_analysis: Moldavian princely court town first attested in 1384 CE; etymology uncertain (possibly Hungarian Horló or Slavic).

b_hotin.first_mention_attestation: Traditional 1001 CE dating as a Kievan Rus' frontier fort is debated in scholarship; firmer documentary attestation begins in the 14th century (1310 CE / List of Russian Cities).

morphemes.translation: personal name Khot / Khoten (from Slavic *xotěti 'to desire')

b_hotin.etymology_analysis: East Slavic possessive toponym from personal name Khot/Khoten + -yn, first chronicled in 1001 CE.

b_tetina.first_mention_attestation: 1325 CE, mentioned as a fort defending the Prut River crossing when Poland seized Galicia.

morphemes.translation: fortress name (from Slavic personal name Čeča / Cecina)

b_tetina.etymology_analysis: Medieval fortress guarding the Prut crossing near Chernivtsi, attested in 1325 CE.

b_cernauti.first_mention_attestation: 1408 CE (8 October 1408), charter of Moldavian Voivode Alexander the Good (as Cernăuți / Chernov'tsi; preceded by 12th-century Galician fort Chern').
b_cernauti.etymology_analysis: Derived from the 12th-century Galician fortress Chern' ('black city', after its dark oak-and-earth walls) + East Slavic/Romanian settlement suffix -ivtsi / -ăuți.

b_piatra_neamnt.first_mention_attestation: 1387–1392 CE, East Slavic chronicle (as Kamena); documented in the 15th century as Piatra lui Crăciun.
b_piatra_neamnt.etymology_analysis: Romanian Piatra ('Stone', translating earlier Slavic Kamena) combined with Neamț (from Slavic *němьcь 'German', referring to the region). Built near the ancient Dacian citadel Petrodava.

historical_names.name: Petrodava
historical_names.source: Ptolemy's Geographia (2nd century CE)
historical_names.notes: Ancient Dacian fortress and political center (Bâtca Doamnei) on the edge of modern Piatra Neamț, flourishing 1st century BCE – 1st century CE.

b_targu_neamnt.first_mention_attestation: 1395 CE (2 February 1395), documentary attestation of the Neamț Citadel and market town.

morphemes.translation: German (referring to the Neamț River / German colonists)

b_targu_neamnt.etymology_analysis: Romanian târg ('market') + Neamț (from Slavic *němьcь 'German', referring to the Neamț River and possible 13th-century Saxon/Teutonic settlers).

b_roman.first_mention_attestation: 1392 CE (30 March 1392), Moldavian charter issued by Voivode Roman I Mușat ('in our fortress of Roman').

eponym.details: Named after Roman I Mușat, Voivode of Moldavia (r. 1391–1394 CE), who founded and fortified the town.

morphemes.translation: personal name of Voivode Roman I Mușat

b_roman.etymology_analysis: Named after Moldavian Voivode Roman I Mușat, who founded the town and issued its first charter in 1392 CE.

b_suceava.first_mention_attestation: 1388 CE (11 February 1388), documentary attestation of Suceava Fortress under Voivode Petru I Mușat.

morphemes.language: Romanian (from Hungarian szűcs 'furrier' or pre-medieval hydronym)
morphemes.translation: name of the Suceava River and city

b_suceava.etymology_analysis: Named after the Suceava River; the medieval fortress and Moldavian capital is first attested in 1388 CE.

b_baia.first_mention_attestation: 1334 CE, Polish/papal document mentioning landowner Alexa Moldaowicz (from Moldenmarkt / Baia).
b_baia.etymology_analysis: From Hungarian bánya / Slavic banja ('mine, quarry'), early Moldavian capital (Civitas Moldaviae / Stadt Molde) attested from 1334 CE.

b_vatra_dornei.first_mention_attestation: 1592 CE, earliest written mention of the settlement.

morphemes.translation: of the Dorna River (genitive of Dorna)

b_vatra_dornei.etymology_analysis: Romanian compound meaning 'Hearth/Core of the Dorna (River)', first attested in 1592 CE.

b_campulung_moldovenesc.first_mention_attestation: 1411 CE (14 April 1411), Moldavian charter of Voivode Alexander the Good.
b_campulung_moldovenesc.etymology_analysis: Romanian Câmpulung ('Long Field') + Moldovenesc ('Moldavian'), first attested in 1411 CE.

b_siret.first_mention_attestation: 1339 CE, earliest historical document mentioning Siret (also listed in 1370–1390 List of Russian Cities).

morphemes.translation: name of the Siret River (ancient Hierasus / Seretos)

b_siret.etymology_analysis: Named after the Siret River; the medieval town of Siret is first attested in 1339 CE.

b_constanta.first_mention_attestation: c. 550 CE, Procopius of Caesarea (De Aedificiis IV.11, as Constantiana, named after Constantia or Constantius II in the 4th century CE); preceded by Tomis from c. 600 BCE.
b_constanta.etymology_analysis: Romanian Constanța evolves directly from Late Roman/Byzantine Constantiana (attested by Procopius c. 550 CE), named in honor of Constantia (half-sister of Constantine the Great) or Constantius II on the site of ancient Greek Tomis.

historical_names.name: Tomis
historical_names.source: Classical Greek sources (Milesian colony founded c. 600 BCE; Ovid's Tristia and Epistulae ex Ponto, 8–17 CE)
historical_names.notes: Ancient Greek polis and Roman capital of Scythia Minor, gradually superseded by the Late Roman name Constantiana.

historical_names.name: Tomi
historical_names.source: Classical Greek sources (Milesian colony founded c. 600 BCE; Ovid's Tristia and Epistulae ex Ponto, 8–17 CE)
historical_names.notes: Ancient Greek polis and Roman capital of Scythia Minor, gradually superseded by the Late Roman name Constantiana.

b_tulcha.first_mention_attestation: 1506 CE, Ottoman records (as Tulcea; preceded by ancient Dacian/Roman Aegyssus).

morphemes.translation: uncertain root (possibly Turkic/Tatar personal or tribal name)

b_tulcha.etymology_analysis: Ottoman-era name Tulcea (attested 1506 CE), likely of Turkic origin, built on the site of ancient Dacian-Roman Aegyssus.

historical_names.name: Aegyssus
historical_names.source: Diodorus Siculus (3rd/1st century BCE); Ovid's Epistulae ex Ponto (1st century CE); Procopius
historical_names.notes: Dacian settlement founded c. 7th century BCE, conquered by Rome in 12–15 CE, abandoned in the 7th century CE.

b_sulina.first_mention_attestation: Mentioned around 950 CE by Byzantine Emperor Constantine VII Porphyrogenitus in De Administrando Imperio as a coastal stop (Sulina) along the route from the Varangians to the Greeks, and later recorded as a 14th-century Genoese port.

morphemes.translation: channel, pipe (Greek solen) or salt marsh (Slavic *solina)

b_sulina.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Sulina distributary of the Danube Delta, variously linked to Byzantine Greek solen ('channel, pipe') or South Slavic *solina ('salt marsh/saline water').

b_mangalia.first_mention_attestation: The name Mangalia is first attested in a document of 1593 CE, superseding earlier medieval names Pangalia and Panglicara.

morphemes.translation: adaptation of Byzantine Greek Pangalia ('most beautiful')

b_mangalia.etymology_analysis: Likely a Tatar/Ottoman phonetic adaptation of medieval Byzantine Greek Pangalia ('the most beautiful'), which succeeded the ancient Greek name Callatis.

historical_names.name: Callatis
historical_names.source: Dorian Greek colony founded by Heraclea Pontica in the 6th century BCE (recorded by Strabo, Pomponius Mela, and Pliny the Elder)
historical_names.notes: Ancient Dorian Greek colony of Callatis (Kallatis), which remained an important Roman and Early Byzantine port before medieval Pangalia and the 1593 CE attestation of Mangalia.

historical_names.name: Kallatis
historical_names.source: Dorian Greek colony founded by Heraclea Pontica in the 6th century BCE (recorded by Strabo, Pomponius Mela, and Pliny the Elder)
historical_names.notes: Ancient Dorian Greek colony of Callatis (Kallatis), which remained an important Roman and Early Byzantine port before medieval Pangalia and the 1593 CE attestation of Mangalia.

historical_names.name: Pangalia
historical_names.source: Dorian Greek colony founded by Heraclea Pontica in the 6th century BCE (recorded by Strabo, Pomponius Mela, and Pliny the Elder)
historical_names.notes: Ancient Dorian Greek colony of Callatis (Kallatis), which remained an important Roman and Early Byzantine port before medieval Pangalia and the 1593 CE attestation of Mangalia.

b_mesembria.first_mention_attestation: Founded as the Dorian Greek colony of Mesembria by Megarian colonists at the beginning of the 6th century BCE on an earlier Thracian settlement, recorded by Herodotus and the Anonymous Periplus.
b_mesembria.etymology_analysis: Hellenized from Thracian *Melsambria / *Menabria, combining a personal/tribal element (traditionally founder Melsas) with Thracian -bria ('town, polis').

b_varna.first_mention_attestation: First attested under the name Varna in 680 CE by Theophanes Confessor, who records Bulgar Khan Asparukh reaching 'the so-called Varna near Odyssos'.
b_varna.etymology_analysis: Disputed origin: variously derived from Proto-Indo-European *uer- ('water, river'), Proto-Slavic *varn- ('black'), Iranian *var ('fortress, camp'), or Old Norse/Varangian värn ('defense').

historical_names.name: Odessos
historical_names.source: Milesian Greek colony founded in the 6th century BCE (attested in the Delian League assessment of 425 BCE)
historical_names.notes: Ancient Thracian settlement and Milesian Greek colony of Odessos (Roman Odessus), superseded by the name Varna in 680 CE.

historical_names.name: Odessus
historical_names.source: Milesian Greek colony founded in the 6th century BCE (attested in the Delian League assessment of 425 BCE)
historical_names.notes: Ancient Thracian settlement and Milesian Greek colony of Odessos (Roman Odessus), superseded by the name Varna in 680 CE.

b_karvuna.first_mention_attestation: Karvuna is attested in the 14th century CE as the regional name (Principality of Karvuna; Italian portolans as Carbona), while Kavarna itself is first mentioned in the 15th century CE.

morphemes.translation: medieval adaptation of ancient Krounoi ('springs'), later influenced by Varna

b_karvuna.etymology_analysis: Karvuna replaced ancient Greek Krounoi (at neighboring Balchik) after the 7th-century Bulgarian conquest; the 15th-century name Kavarna likely arose by phonetic contamination between Karvuna and Varna.

historical_names.name: Bizone
historical_names.source: Greek colony of Bizone founded by colonists from Mesembria in the 5th–4th century BCE
historical_names.notes: Ancient Thracian settlement (9th–7th century BCE) and Greek colony of Bizone on the Kavarna coast, destroyed in the 7th century CE.

historical_names.name: Byzone
historical_names.source: Greek colony of Bizone founded by colonists from Mesembria in the 5th–4th century BCE
historical_names.notes: Ancient Thracian settlement (9th–7th century BCE) and Greek colony of Bizone on the Kavarna coast, destroyed in the 7th century CE.

b_barlad.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in documentary sources in 1174 CE (and securely attested as a Moldavian market town by 1401–1408 CE).
b_barlad.etymology_analysis: Named after the Bârlad River (historically associated with the medieval Berladnici); proposed etymologies include Slavic or Cuman/Turkic roots.

b_vaslui.first_mention_attestation: First attested in historical documents in 1375 CE as a settlement in the Principality of Moldavia.
b_vaslui.etymology_analysis: Named after the Vaslui (Vasluieț) River; the -ui ending is characteristic of Cuman/Pecheneg hydronyms in Moldavia ('water, river').

b_husi.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in a letter of 17 December 1487 CE sent by Stephen III the Great of Moldavia to the Saxon merchants of Brașov.

morphemes.translation: from Hussites or personal name Husul

b_husi.etymology_analysis: Traditionally derived either from 15th-century Hussite refugees who settled in Moldavia or from a Moldavian boyar named Husul attested in 1495–1502 CE.

b_galati.first_mention_attestation: First attested under the name Galați in a 1445 CE document signed by Stephen II of Moldavia.

morphemes.translation: from Cuman galat ('fortress', via Arabic qal'at) or Little Halych / Slavic gal-

b_galati.etymology_analysis: Disputed etymology: most scholars link Galați to Cuman galat ('fortress', from Persian/Arabic qal'at) or to 13th-century Galician-Volhynian influence ('Little Halych').

historical_names.name: Barboși
historical_names.source: Roman castrum at Tirighina-Barboși built after Trajan's Dacian Wars (101–106 CE) on an earlier Dacian settlement
historical_names.notes: Roman frontier castrum at Barboși guarding the Siret–Danube confluence and a Daco-Roman settlement at the Danube ford predated medieval Galați.

historical_names.name: Tirighina-Barboși
historical_names.source: Roman castrum at Tirighina-Barboși built after Trajan's Dacian Wars (101–106 CE) on an earlier Dacian settlement
historical_names.notes: Roman frontier castrum at Barboși guarding the Siret–Danube confluence and a Daco-Roman settlement at the Danube ford predated medieval Galați.

b_tecuci.first_mention_attestation: First attested on 1 September 1435 CE in a letter from Voivode Iliaș of Moldavia to King Władysław of Poland granting Tecuci to his brother Stephen.

morphemes.translation: flowing water (Slavic tek-) or border/end (Turkic tehek-uciu)

b_tecuci.etymology_analysis: Named after the Tecuci stream; Iorgu Iordan and Ion Bogdan derive it from Slavic tek- ('to flow'), while Alexandru Philippide proposed a Pecheneg-Cuman compound meaning 'border/end of the land'.

b_focsani.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in Brașov customs registers of 1546 CE (as Fokschein) and in a Wallachian charter of 30 January 1575 CE.
b_focsani.etymology_analysis: Romanian collective toponym in -ani, traditionally linked to a putative Focșa family from the era of Stephen the Great.

b_iasi.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1396 CE by the German crusader Johann Schiltberger, and first recorded in an official Moldavian document in 1408 CE.
b_iasi.etymology_analysis: Derived from the ethnonym of the Alanic Jász (medieval Iranian/Alanic tribe; cf. Hungarian Jászvásár 'Jász market'), or less likely from the ancient Sarmatian Iazyges.

b_ungheni.first_mention_attestation: First historical mention of Ungheni dates to 20 August 1462 CE in a Moldavian document.
b_ungheni.etymology_analysis: Romanian toponym in -eni from unghi ('corner, bend'), referring to a bend in the Prut River.

b_falesti.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in a 1429 CE document of Moldavian ruler Alexander the Good (with secure later attestation in 1614 CE).
b_falesti.etymology_analysis: Standard Romanian patronymic/clan toponym formed with the plural suffix -ești.

b_orhei.first_mention_attestation: Medieval Moldavian town of Orhei was built soon after 1368 CE at Orheiul Vechi on the remains of the Golden Horde town Shehr al-Jedid; modern Orhei was established nearby in the 16th century.
b_orhei.etymology_analysis: Borrowed into Romanian as Orhei from Hungarian Őrhely ('guard post, watchtower'), reflecting medieval frontier fortifications along the Răut River.

b_tuzara.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 1432–1433 CE when Voivode Ilie of Moldavia granted the village of Tuzara (predecessor of Călărași, Moldova) to his servant Staia.
b_tuzara.etymology_analysis: Medieval Moldavian village name on the Bâc River, likely of Turkic (Cuman/Tatar) origin from tuz ('salt').

b_soroca.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 1499 CE when Moldavian Prince Stephen the Great built a wooden fort at the Dniester ford, succeeding the medieval Genoese trading post of Olchionia (Alchona).

morphemes.translation: magpie (Slavic soroka) or Romanian soroc ('term, appointed place')

b_soroca.etymology_analysis: Uncertain origin; commonly compared to East Slavic soroka ('magpie') or Romanian soroc ('appointed term/station').

b_balti.first_mention_attestation: First attested on 4 October 1620 CE in Polish campaign accounts along the Răut River (the 1421 CE Ringala attribution is a modern confusion with Belz).
b_balti.etymology_analysis: Plural of Romanian baltă ('puddle, marsh', a Dacian/Balkan substrate word), referring to the marshy confluence of the Răuțel and Răut rivers.

b_stoenesti.first_mention_attestation: Medieval Romanian village name attested from the 16th century (e.g., 9 June 1507 CE for Stoenești, Vâlcea; 19 May 1565 CE for Stoenești, Argeș).
b_stoenesti.etymology_analysis: Romanian patronymic toponym formed from the personal name Stoian (of South Slavic origin, 'steadfast') plus the collective/estate suffix -ești.

b_bacau.first_mention_attestation: First appeared in documentary records in 1408 CE as an important Moldavian customs point.

morphemes.translation: medieval personal name Bakó (of Cuman/Pecheneg or Hungarian origin)

b_bacau.etymology_analysis: Probably derived from a medieval personal name of Hungarian or Cuman/Pecheneg origin (Bakó, attested in Old Church Slavonic as Bako/Bakova), or alternatively from Proto-Slavic *byk ('ox, bull').

b_braila.first_mention_attestation: First certain documentary mention is a 20 January 1368 CE commercial privilege issued by Vladislav I of Wallachia to Brașov merchants (as Braylan); earlier Catalan portolans (1325–1339) list Drinago.
b_braila.etymology_analysis: Origin uncertain; widely considered to derive from an anthroponym (or Slavic *Brailov, cf. Greek Proilavon), though older theories proposed an Indo-European root *bhreg- ('steep bank').

b_ramnicu_sarat.first_mention_attestation: First attested in a Wallachian commercial privilege dated 8 September 1439 CE.
b_ramnicu_sarat.etymology_analysis: Named after the Râmnicul Sărat River: Râmnic comes from Slavic *rybnik ('fishpond, fish-bearing stream') and Sărat ('salty') distinguishes it from Râmnicu Vâlcea.

b_bucuresti.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned on 20 September 1459 CE in a charter of Prince Vlad III Dracula as the Citadel of București.
b_bucuresti.etymology_analysis: Romanian collective toponym in -ești from the personal name Bucur (traditionally linked to a legendary shepherd Bucur).

b_targsor.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned as a settlement in a charter issued on 6 August 1413 CE by Voivode Mircea the Elder of Wallachia.
b_targsor.etymology_analysis: Diminutive of Romanian târg ('market town', from South Slavic), meaning 'little market'.

b_buzau.first_mention_attestation: First documented as a Wallachian market town (târg) and customs point in a 1431 CE charter of Prince Dan II.

morphemes.translation: from ancient river name Mousaios / Thracian *Bouzeos

b_buzau.etymology_analysis: Named after the Buzău River, identified with the ancient Mousaios (Mouseos) attested in 376 CE (proposed by Vasile Pârvan as a Greek transcription of Thracian *Bouzeos).

historical_names.name: Mousaios
historical_names.source: Letter of Ioannis Soranus, governor of Scythia Minor (c. 376–400 CE, Passion of Saint Sabbas the Goth)
historical_names.notes: The river Mousaios (Buzău) and a settlement/polis on its banks are attested in 376 CE in connection with the 372 CE martyrdom of Sabbas the Goth.

historical_names.name: Mouseos
historical_names.source: Letter of Ioannis Soranus, governor of Scythia Minor (c. 376–400 CE, Passion of Saint Sabbas the Goth)
historical_names.notes: The river Mousaios (Buzău) and a settlement/polis on its banks are attested in 376 CE in connection with the 372 CE martyrdom of Sabbas the Goth.

b_slobozia.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 1594 CE under the name Vaideei in a charter of Michael the Brave, and as Slobozia in March 1614 CE under Radu Mihnea.

morphemes.translation: tax-exempt newly colonized village (from Slavic slobod 'free')

b_slobozia.etymology_analysis: From Romanian slobozie ('tax-free settlement'), itself borrowed from Slavic slobod ('free'), referring to tax exemptions granted to repopulate the Bărăgan Plain.

historical_names.name: Netindava
historical_names.source: Ptolemy's Geographia (2nd century CE); cited by Encyclopaedia Britannica as the ancient predecessor at Slobozia
historical_names.notes: Encyclopaedia Britannica notes that modern Slobozia was built on remains associated with the Dacian/Roman settlement of Netindava.

b_ploiesti.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in documentary records in 1503 CE as a village in Muntenia, before being made a market town (târg) by Michael the Brave in 1597 CE.
b_ploiesti.etymology_analysis: Romanian patronymic toponym in -ești, traditionally derived from a founder's personal name Ploaie (Moș Ploae).

b_calarasi.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 1593 CE as the village of Lichirești under Michael the Brave; the name Călărași first appeared on Constantin Cantacuzino's 1700 CE map.

morphemes.translation: mounted couriers, horsemen (plural of călăraș, from cal 'horse')

b_calarasi.etymology_analysis: Named after the călărași (mounted royal couriers) stationed at Lichirești along the post route between Bucharest and Istanbul.

b_radovanu.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation; modern Romanian commune in Călărași County (archaeological Geto-Dacian dava sites at Gorgana I–II lack an attested ancient name).
b_radovanu.etymology_analysis: Derived from the South Slavic/Romanian personal name Radovan.

b_fetesti.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1528 CE in a document issued by Wallachian ruler Radu of Afumați.
b_fetesti.etymology_analysis: Romanian patronymic toponym formed with the plural suffix -ești.

b_giurgiu.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in Codex Latinus Parisinus in 1395 CE during the reign of Mircea the Elder (and in a Wallachian charter of 23 September 1403 CE).

morphemes.translation: George (after Genoa's patron saint San Giorgio)

b_giurgiu.etymology_analysis: Old Romanian form of George, named after Saint George (San Giorgio), patron saint of Genoa, by 14th-century Genoese merchants.

historical_names.name: Daphne
historical_names.source: Late Roman Danubian fort built under Constantine the Great (c. 328 CE; attested by Ammianus Marcellinus in 367 CE)
historical_names.notes: Late Roman/Byzantine Danubian bridgehead fort of Daphne, located on the lower Danube in the Giurgiu–Oltenița sector.

b_turnu.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 1387–1394 CE as Turnu (Nicopolis Minor / Little Nicopolis) under Mircea the Elder.
b_turnu.etymology_analysis: From Romanian turn ('tower', from Latin turris), referring to the medieval fortress (later paired with Măgurele 'hillocks' in 1836).

historical_names.name: Turris
historical_names.source: Procopius of Caesarea (De Aedificiis, c. 550 CE), attributing the foundation of Turris to Emperor Trajan
historical_names.notes: Roman-Byzantine fortress of Turris near the Olt–Danube confluence, attested by Procopius in the 6th century CE.

b_rusii_de_vede.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1385 CE by two German pilgrims returning from Jerusalem as Russenart (historically Rușii de Vede).
b_rusii_de_vede.etymology_analysis: Originally Rușii de Vede ('the Russians on the Vedea'), later reshaped as Roșiorii de Vede ('the Redcoat cavalry on the Vedea').

b_comana.first_mention_attestation: First attested on 27 September 1461 CE in a donation charter of Prince Vlad III Dracula for Comana Monastery.
b_comana.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Romanian personal name Coman (reflecting medieval Cuman presence in Wallachia).

b_glavacioc.first_mention_attestation: First attested in a Wallachian document dated 14 April 1441 CE (with Glavacioc Monastery founded under Mircea the Elder).
b_glavacioc.etymology_analysis: Named after the Glavacioc River, from South Slavic glava ('head, source').

b_costesti.first_mention_attestation: First documented on 30 July 1535 CE in a deed issued by Wallachian Voivode Radu Paisie.
b_costesti.etymology_analysis: Romanian patronymic toponym formed from the personal name Costea plus the suffix -ești.
